items.title: Yankees get outplayed by Rasmussen, Rays in Game 1 of ALDS
items.author: Dani Mohr
items.content:
The Yankees came into the ALDS riding high, having crushed their archrivals in the Wild Card Series, the lineup coming alive just in time. Unfortunately, just as quickly as they woke up, the bats fell asleep, no match for Rays ace Drew Rasmussen in a 1-0 shutout loss to Tampa Bay.

New York’s downfall started (and in a way ended) when Gerrit Cole gave up a solo home run in the third, the primary blemish in what was a five-inning outing with five hits and one earned run. Cole left a changeup over the middle of the plate, and Jonathan Aranda sent a deep fly into the right-field seats:

Cole was replaced by Ryan Weathers, who made his return to the mound after a stint on the injured list with a left elbow injury, and didn’t allow the Rays’ offense to inflict any more damage. Paul Blackburn replaced Weathers in the bottom of the seventh and recorded one walk in 1.2 innings. Brent Headrick followed, who walked one batter before escaping with two runners on to end the eighth.

As for the Yankees offense, well, there isn’t much to speak of, as the lineup Boone sent out simply couldn’t make any headway against the Rays’ elite pitching staff. Rasmussen ended up pitching eight scoreless innings, allowing only one hit and two walks, completely shutting down the Yankees’ ambitions of getting ahead early in the series. Rasmussen kept the Yankees not just out of the run column, but blanked them in the hit column until the eighth, missing a no-hitter by just four outs as Austin Wells broke things up with a two-out double in the eighth.

Yet that moment also brought one of the most notable errors in the Yankees’ decision-making, with Wells attempting to stretch his double into a triple. His speed wasn’t enough to get him to third, and the Yankees’ catcher got thrown out to end the inning. Victor Mesa made the throw to shortstop Taylor Walls, who immediately tagged Wells as he went for the slide. An aerial view showed that third base coach Luis Rojas was trying to hold Wells up, so it really was just Wells inexplicably attempting to get to third base with two outs:

It’s worth noting that Giancarlo Stanton made his first appearance at the plate since April, pinch-hitting for Ryan McMahon, and sadly struck out in four pitches from Rays reliever Bryan Baker as the Yankees’ attempt at a ninth-inning rally went nowhere fast, Baker also striking out Ben Rice and getting Cody Bellinger to ground out to end the game.

Though the Yankees may be on the road and striving for a victory in Game 2, it remains to be seen whether Boone will change the lineup and experiment with other position players to shuffle the order. There wasn’t much to smile about today, with the small exceptions of Stanton’s cameo appearance, and the solid showing from Weathers after a layoff. Sunday will give the Yankees another day of rest to regroup. Hopefully, we’ll see a different result come Monday.

items.title: Jenny Rissveds and Luca Martin secure 2026 Mountain Bike World Series overall cross-country titles
items.author: Lyne Lamoureux
items.content:
Jenny Rissveds (Canyon XC Racing) and Luca Martin (Cannondale Factory Racing) were awarded the 2026 Mountain Bike World Cup (XCO) cross-country overall series titles as the competition wrapped up at Lake Placid Olympic Sites, New York, on Saturday. Both riders came into the final round assured of the overall victory as long as they finished the race. 

Both the women’s and men’s races came down to a sprint battle after a dynamic final lap of racing, as dry, sunny conditions greeted riders, a stark contrast to Friday, when they battled a wet and muddy course where Martina Berta (Origine Racing) and Martin Vidaurre (Specialized Factory Racing) claimed the respective XCC victories.

Distanced early in the women’s race, Rissveds finished 11th, over two minutes behind winner Sina Frei (Specialized Factory Racing), who edged Berta in a two-up sprint, throwing her bike to the line to claim the elite women’s victory with Maxwell finishing third.

“I was considering to just start [the race] and and pull over and wait for them to lap me and to get pulled, but I thought at least I try, and I tried. I wouldn't say I gave up butI had to settle in like halfway through. It was way too fast for me today,” Rissveds said.

“The level is incredibly high at the moment, and only compared to last year, it's much faster, and the racing is a lot tighter. The other teams have done their homework over winter, and that's what we have to do to keep up with them for the coming years.”

The first split occurred early the first time the riders tackled the technical rock garden, with a front group of 12 riders dwindling to seven halfway through the race. Joining world champion Frei, Berta and Maxwell in the lead group were Gwendalyn Gibson (Trek Unbroken), Alessandra Keller (Thömus Maxon), Nicole Koller (Lapierre PXR Racing), and Laura Stigger (Specialized Factory Racing).

By the final lap, only Frei, Berta and Maxwell remained in contention for the win. Frei took control at the front, while Maxwell accelerated on the climbs but could not get around her and slotted into third wheel as they tackled the uphill rock garden. Berta then bobbled, forcing Maxwell to stop behind her as Frei opened a gap and seemed on her way to a solo victory.

But Berta refused to give up, catching Frei before the final straight. The pair sprinted for the win, with Berta slowly gaining on the Swiss rider, but Frei took the win.

“I was sprinting full gas, and I saw the wheel coming, and I was like, ‘no, faster, faster, more, more, more’, and then I just pushed the bike to the front, and I'm so happy that it worked,” Frei said. 

“I'm so so happy, starting the season and finishing the season with a win is incredible.” Frei added. “The first one I won with the team jersey, second one with the European [jersey], and the third one with the World Champ jersey. It's incredible.”

Inspired by its bobsled heritage, the short, fast and technical Mt Van Hoevenberg’s XCC course combined wide ski trails with twisting singletrack, punchy climbs, bermed corners, rocks, roots and a distinctive jump section.

In the final race for the Cannondale Factory Racing team, which is folding at the end of the year, Martin finished fifth, 20 seconds behind the winner, his teammate Charlie Aldridge. The British rider outsprinted Filippo Colombo (Scott-Sram MTB Racing Team) to claim his first World Cup win since his victory at the final 2025 race at Mont-Sainte-Anne. Vidaurre finished third.

“It’s so cool, to be on the podium is quite special. Today, we finished so well, three guys on the top five. I can tell you it was pretty hard,” Martin said.

Colombo went out hard early, applying pressure at the front, with a lead group of seven pulling away halfway through the nine-lap race. Along with Aldridge, Colombo and Vidaurre, the split included Fabio Püntener (Scott-Sram MTB Racing Team), Simone Avondetto (Wilier-Vittora Factory Team), Cole Punchard (Cannondale Factory Racing)  and Martin.

Attacks continued to fly as the seven raced into the final lap. First Vidaurre, then Colombo put in massive accelerations until finally Aldridge made his move, launching early and leading into the finish straight, where he was able to hold off the others to take the win.

“I finally won a sprint. I went too early, too late, this time was perfect, and I'm buzzing with that. Last race of the year, what a way to finish it off,” Aldridge said.

“It’s just a lovely way to finish the last race for Cannondale-Factory Racing, and it feels great to finish off at a high.”

items.title: AL Division Series Game 1: Gerrit Cole vs. Drew Rasmussen
items.author: Dani Mohr
items.content:
The Yankees will kick off the Division Series from Tampa, with Gerrit Cole on the mound and Ben Rice leading off as the Bombers look to continue the chase for 28.

Going with yet another lefty-heavy lineup, the Yankees are going with Jazz Chisholm Jr. at second, Spencer Jones in right field, and Luis García Jr. at first over Paul Goldschmidt. The veteran first baseman may appear as a pinch-hitter, as may Giancarlo Stanton, who is on the roster again but won’t start.

Drew Rasmussen will get his second career postseason outing for the Rays, looking for a hot start to the series in Tampa Bay. The 31-year-old righty had a 2.67 ERA in 30 starts during the regular season. He’s posting a 2.86 ERA against the Yankees this season, allowing 14 hits and giving up seven earned runs in 22 innings.

We hope that you’ll come join us in the game thread as we kick off another postseason matchup as the Yankees race for the American League!

items.title: Yankees reveal lineup for Game 1 of ALDS vs. Rays
items.author: Dani Mohr
items.content:
The Yankees are set to continue their postseason run, and have revealed their lineup for Game 1 of the Division Series from Tampa Bay.

Ben Rice leads off for the Yankees after dominating the Red Sox in the Wild Card Series, with expectations to continue his hot streak against the Rays. Bellinger will bat second with García Jr. in the hole, seemingly unchanged from the Game 2 lineup that secured the sweep against Boston.

Spencer Jones will hit cleanup in the order and start in right over Heliot Ramos, followed by George Lombard Jr. and Jazz Chisholm Jr., who will get the start at second over Anthony Volpe. Trent Grisham will notably get the start at center field, with Austin Wells unsurprisingly starting behind the plate.

As confirmed ahead of the postseason matchup, Gerrit Cole will start on the mound as the Yankees look to earn a series opener win.

Here’s a look at the Rays’ starting lineup, which puts Yandy Díaz in the leadoff spot followed by Jonathan Aranda and Junior Caminero.

items.title: Evans set for “all in or nothing” approach to WRC title showdown
Cholet Agglo Tour: Jenthe Biermans wins from break after massive pull from teammate Bryan Coquard
items.author: Lyne Lamoureux
items.content:
Benefitting from the work of Cofidis teammate Bryan Coquard, Jenthe Biermans outsprinted his breakaway companions to win Cholet Agglo Tour on Saturday.  

Coquard initiated the four-rider break with 18 kilometres to go and then buried himself for his teammate. The move also included Matyáš Kopecký (Unibet Rose Rochets) and Axel Huens (Groupama-FDJ United), who would take second and third, respectively, as Coquard celebrated his teammate’s victory crossing the line in fourth place.

“I was feeling really good. I saw that Bryan attacked, he was followed, there was a bit of hesitation and I made the jump. So, we ended up with two of us there, which made the finale easier, though we really had to ride hard because the group was almost catching us,” Biermans said.

“In the final three kilometres, he told me, ‘okay, I’ll sacrifice myself for you, after everything you’ve done for me this year.’ I said, ‘okay, I’ll win this for you.’ The plan was perfect and thanks to the whole team.”

“Bryan is a great teammate and a great leader and what he did today, I will never forget. Thanks to him.”

The pack faced a 197km course in and out of Cholet, as part of the FDJ United Series, formerly known as the Coupe de France. The first 150 kilometres looped around the greater urban area on rolling terrain typical of the roads of Maine-et-Loire before returning to Cholet. Then the riders took on a twisty 8km urban circuit a total of five times.

Early in the race, five riders made it into the break, with Victor Jean (Elite Foundations) collecting top KOM points over the 10 categorised climbs. Behind, Unibet Rose Rockets kept a tight leash on the gap, keeping it at around the 2-minute mark for defending champion Lukáš Kubiš.

The action really started to kick off as the break down to two riders with Léandre Huck (Van Rysel-Roubaix) and Jean, who made their way into the finishing circuit only to be reeled in with 30 kilometres to go.

Around 10 kilometres later, Coquard put in a massive acceleration that was quickly covered by Kopecký, with Biermans and Huens bridging across.

With nine kilometres to go, the quartet held a 19-second advantage over a reshuffling chase group, and managed to stay away.

items.title: A full breakdown of the Yankees’ Division Series roster
items.author: Dani Mohr
items.content:
The stage is set for the Postseason, and the Yankees have confirmed their 26-man roster for the American League Division Series.

There isn’t too much of a change from the Wild Card Series roster, but it’s worth noting that Aaron Judge is left out once again, and Ryan Weathers is available to step in as a reliever for the first time since late August. The lefty pitcher was placed on the IL with a left forearm flexor strain. The Yankees also left out third baseman Amed Rosario to make room for Weathers on the roster.

Here’s everything you need to know about each player and how they can propel the Yankees’ postseason run in the ALDS against Tampa Bay.

The Yankees will rely on Bellinger to give the offense some momentum, especially without Aaron Judge. He went 3-for-9 in the Wild Card Series with a home run that sealed the victory for the Yankees in Game 2. If he can stay hot in Tampa Bay, it should be enough to keep the Pinstripes on top.

A utilityman most likely to be deployed at third base, Caballero has the potential to be effective defensively and may get the start over Ryan McMahon. He finished September batting .163 with a .260 OBP, but didn’t get any at-bats during the Wild Card Series against Boston.

Jazz will likely play second in higher risk scenarios and alternate with Anthony Volpe. He went 2-for-3 with two runs and worked a walk in Game 2 of the Wild Card Series.

After drilling a home run that helped the Yankees dominate Boston in Game 2, García Jr. will look to keep his numbers up against the Rays. He will likely alternate with Paul Goldschmidt, who does well against lefties.

Serving as a reliable option at first base, Goldschmidt brings a strong veteran presence that sets the tone for the younger guys on the roster. He worked two walks late in Game 1 of the Wild Card Series that gave Ben Rice the perfect setup for the grand slam.

After making his return from the IL in the Wild Card Series, Grisham will likely alternate at center field with Spencer Jones. It’s unclear if the Yankees will use him as a starter against Tampa Bay over Jones, but keeping him available to pinch hit could be the best option.

Following his postseason debut, Jones will likely continue to build off his momentum as the Yankees head to Tampa Bay. However, if he ends up struggling to make an impact offensively, it wouldn’t be surprising to see a pinch hitter like Stanton take his place in the order.

A standout in the Wild Card Series, Lombard Jr. instills confidence defensively while also remaining fearless at the plate. He went 4-for-8 against Boston with three runs, and can give the Yankees support towards the middle of the order.

Alternating with Caballero at third, McMahon is expected to make a start at least once against Tampa to test the options at third base.

Although he didn’t play a huge role in giving the Yankees insurance against Boston, Ramos will likely start at right field if the Rays throw out a left-handed starter and otherwise prepare to get hot off the bench in the ALDS. There’s also a chance that he alternates with Spencer Jones in the field. After a bit of a cold start in Pinstripes, Ramos finished September batting .255 with a .491 slugging percentage.

What else is there to say about Rice other than that he’s been the most clutch hitter for the Yankees without Aaron Judge? There’s no doubt we’ve seen the last of his electricity at the plate, and it’ll be very exciting to see how he matches up against the Rays.

Available as a backup for Austin Wells behind the plate, it’s unsurprising that Sánchez made the roster and has the chance to appear in a low-risk scenario.

Despite not getting the chance to hit in the Wild Card Series, Stanton will likely have a pinch hitting opportunity in the ALDS. One of the Yankees’ all-time leading playoff sluggers, with 18 homers, Big G might have his classic playoff moment that will leave the Rays stunned.

After hitting a sacrifice bunt in Game 1 of the Wild Card Series that helped set the Yankees up to shut down Boston, Volpe has the potential to shine against the Rays. He will alternate with Jazz at second, and we will likely see him get the start at least once in the series.

After jumpstarting the Yankees offense that totaled 18 runs in the two-game Wild Card Series sweep, Wells will look to bring the same energy against Tampa Bay. It will be fun to see him hopefully win an ABS challenge.

Maintaining his spot on the roster as the Yankees’ closer, Bednar wasn’t needed in the Wild Card Series but got some work to stay fresh in Game 2. He’ll be prepared to earn the save against Tampa Bay should the Yankees enter the ninth with a lead and continue the chase for 28.

After giving up a hit in Game 1 of the Wild Card Series and inducing a double play that ended the seventh, Blackburn is prepared to make an impact in quieting the Tampa Bay offense.

Getting the start for Game 1 of the ALDS, Cole will look to dominate the Rays in his first postseason outing since 2024. If needed, he will also likely be available for the Game 4 start.

Effectively shutting down Boston’s offense in the Wild Card Series, Fried will likely start Game 3 and hopefully keep the Rays’ offense at bay.

Maintaining consistency throughout the regular season, Headrick is expected to shine in a relief role throughout the postseason. He finished the regular season with a 2.18 ERA and 98 strikeouts over 78.3 innings. Headrick was used a lot, but did at least get three full days of rest going into today.

If we don’t end up seeing him in a starting role, Rodón is expected to come in as a reliever and shut down the Tampa Bay offense. He didn’t make an appearance against Boston, but if he can keep his numbers from September trending in the right direction, he’ll be lights out.

Dominating Boston in Game 1, and continuing his feud with seemingly the entire state of Massachusetts, Schlittler will surely be one of the Yankees’ most powerful weapons on the bump. The 25-year-old ace is poised to make his second career ALDS appearance as a starter for Game 2 and could be available for a decisive Game 5 should this series go the distance.

Taking a spot as a relief option if needed, Schreiber may take the mound in a low-risk scenario.

Giving up a run in 1.2 innings of Game 2 in the Wild Card Series, Warren will look to bounce back and silence the bats from Tampa Bay. One of the team’s core starters all year, Warren started transitioning into a role with the bullpen through a couple appearances in September and his presence as a multi-inning option is one of the reasons the Yankees can so confidently field an extended bench.

Positioned to make his first relief appearance since being reinstated from the IL, Weathers will be a crucial addition to this roster in place of third baseman Amed Rosario. He showed promising signs in his bullpen sessions, and we’ll expect him to be an essential factor in shutting down the Rays’ offense. Weathers was another starter alongside Warren making the shift over, though he has some experience relieving as he made 12 appearances out of the ‘pen in his rookie season with the Padres.

Securing his spot on the roster over Tim Hill, Yarbrough will be available as a low-risk option, and he could make an appearance on the bump if there’s a scenario where they need to get a reliever out of a jam.

items.title: Arizona Fall League 2026 preview
items.author: Michael Zeno
items.content:
The minor league season has officially concluded league-wide, with the Triple-A Championship Game on September 26th officially serving as the conclusion of the final game in Minor League Baseball in 2026. As thousands of players across all levels prepare for their offseason, there exists a handful in every organization who aren’t quite done with organized ball yet.

That is where we find the Arizona Fall League, which will be running for the 34th season since its founding in 1992 as an opportunity for an assortment of prospects to gain additional in-game experience. It’s often used by organizations to compensate for lost time due to injury, give experience to lower-minor prospects against stiffer competition, or to use it as an extra opportunity to tweak or introduce something in a low-stakes environment.

The Yankees have sent players of all shapes and sizes to this, from non-prospects deep into the organizational depth chart to highly touted prospects like Aaron Judge, Gleyber Torres, Jasson Domínguez, and Alfonso Soriano. Two years ago, current Boston rival Caleb Durbin got himself on the map with a huge performance, proving that this stage can positively impact prospect buzz.

For those unfamiliar with the format, the league’s 30 teams are divided into six AFL clubs, which have a 35-man roster and contain the contingents from five different organizations. It changes every year, so the one that the eight Yankees representatives will be going to is the , alongside prospects from the Twins, Rockies, Diamondbacks, and Nationals.

With the AFL officially kicking off today at 3:30 p.m. EDT in Glendale, let’s meet the eight-man Yankees contingent:

The prized prospect of the bunch, Dax Kilby will headline the group. The 2025 first-round pick stole headlines with an incredible 19-game cup of coffee in Single-A Tampa last August that vaulted him onto Top 100 lists and raised high expectations for his first full professional season at age 19, but such a season was doomed from the start.

A hamstring injury suffered early in spring held him out of the Spring Breakout game in March and delayed his season debut until May 28th, but there was still plenty of runway from there. Unfortunately, after taking just two at-bats, he suffered a setback that held him out an additional six weeks. He finally returned for good on July 17th, but was limited to just 36 total games in what was supposed to be a big season for him. It comes as no surprise, then, that he’s getting extra reps here in Arizona.

In his extremely limited time at Tampa this season, Kilby was effective, slashing .261/.448/.435 with a 143 wRC+ in 154 plate appearances. He boasts an extremely mature approach at the plate, walking in a quarter of his plate appearances, but has yet to really tap into the power. He’s above-average at pretty much everything, something you love to see from a 19-year-old, but you’re looking for the standout trait.

Something to monitor in this, aside from how he performs against older pitching, will be his defense. He’s never been considered likely to stick at shortstop, but is a good enough athlete to feasibly play second base, third base, or even center field. We’ll see if he’s moved around or if one of the best prospects in all of the AFL will just get to man shortstop the entire time.

Every year, you’ll see the Yankees send one or two guys to the AFL who don’t have much of a pro sample to go off of. This year’s version of that is Mack Estrada, the team’s 11th-round pick in 2024, who has just 4.1 professional innings through the first 2.5 seasons of his professional career.

Estrada is a guy that the Yanks invested a lot in, giving him a massive overslot of $640,340, the fifth-highest in the class, to get him out of a commit to go to Florida State out of junior college. He, like the rest of the team’s draft-year pitchers, was shut down to end the 2024 season, but went under the knife early in 2025 and missed the next season and a half due to Tommy John surgery.

He only got back to pitch in four games this summer with the FCL Yankees, where he struggled in a bunch of small, choppy outings. He’s spent the last two months in the complex, so we’ll see if he’s being utilized as a multi-inning guy in the AFL.

What can we expect from him? We don’t have data on how his stuff has looked post-TJS, but he’s more of a fastball/slider guy who was capable of getting it up to 96 on the heater in college. The Yankees love to tinker with young pitcher’s arsenals, so we’ll see if he has another offering or two.

A handful of the players in this year’s AFL contingent missed time in the last two years due to injury, but few were able to get back from those injuries with enough time to be as impactful as J.T. Etheridge was.

An undrafted free agent out of Louisiana in 2024, Etheridge started his pro career strong in the FCL in May 2025, but struggled after a promotion to Tampa late in the season. His 2026 started as more of the same, pitching to a 6.51 ERA deep into August. As a prospect without much invested in you, it’s a dangerous game to play going into an offseason with zero production above rookie ball at 25, which he’ll be in January.

The fact he’s here in Arizona, though, shows that he did make some progress. Something seemed to click in mid-August, when he suddenly became the unlikely ace of a Tampa team that came within a game of a Florida State League championship. In his last six starts, he allowed just one run in 27 innings with 38 strikeouts, including a pair of scoreless playoff outings. The decision to send him came before a few of these outings, so the belief might’ve been there even longer.

He boasted an impressive 32.9 strikeout rate with great whiff rates. He sits at 94 on his four-seam fastball and has both a sweeper and a slider that grade well above average. The damage off him primarily comes from the curveball and sinker, which he throws a combined 23 percent of the time. Expect him to tinker with those this fall.

While Kilby is the much more important prospect for Yankees fans to monitor this fall, I’d argue that the guy I’m most excited to see get extra reps here is Antonio Gomez. You may remember that name from a couple of years ago as a defense-first catcher whose bat never quite caught up with him. Yes, that is that same kid.

Gomez was floundering at Double-A Somerset in June 2025 when he was placed on the Development List. While that is usually a death sentence for any prospect, Gomez was different. Instead of being in organizational limbo, he was switching professions, going from a catcher with an 80-grade arm to a flamethrowing reliever. He made his pitching debut a month later and lit up the radar guns, but underwent elbow surgery after just four outings.

He returned this August and has just been trying to get into a rhythm as a pitcher. He’s only tossed 8.1 total innings across 10 career outings, so any experience he can get here in Arizona is extremely valuable. The thing that tickles your fancy about him is his alien fastball, which sits in the upper 90s with over 20 inches of induced vertical break, something you pretty much never see in the bigs:

A late addition to the roster, Anthony Mena signed as an older international signing in 2024 at the age of 19 and didn’t make his stateside debut until 2026 after two solid years in the DSL. In 2025, he struck out 57 in 45.2 innings with a 3.11 ERA.

The results were pretty rough in his 16.2 innings in the FCL early this summer, but he got an aggressive promotion to Tampa midway through the season after a mountain of injuries completely destroyed their pitching depth. His stuff hasn’t quite caught up yet, but he did pretty well after the promotion, allowing just three runs in 16.1 innings across five multi-inning outings.

He leans on his low-90s sinker, throwing it 44 percent of the time, while supplementing it with a changeup, slider, and curveball, with the latter two generating the best results.

Our last pitcher of the bunch, Chris Veach, is the only one who isn’t extremely early in their development as a Single-A pitcher. A 2024 undrafted free agent out of South Carolina, Veach graduated from Tampa in 2025 after a terrific season, pitching to a 2.53 ERA with 75 strikeouts in 57 innings.

This year has been a much more difficult season for him, but not because of anything on the field. The 25-year-old missed nine weeks with an undisclosed injury in the summer, shortly after earning a promotion to Double-A Somerset in June. He was only able to get into 25 games and throw 29 innings, but he excelled while doing so, pitching to a 1.86 ERA with 39 strikeouts to 10 walks. He’ll be 26 in a month and a half, so the extra development will be very helpful for him.

We don’t have arsenal stats for High-A and Double-A, but a look at Veach’s repertoire shows he utilizes a heavy diet of changeups that is backed up by a trio of fastballs. Things might’ve changed in the last year, but he threw a breaking ball just 0.8 percent of the time last season. Could that be something they ask him to work on in the desert?

Finally, to the position players. Core Jackson is the second-biggest name value prospect they’re sending to Arizona this fall. The 2025 fifth-round pick had a strong debut season in the system, splitting time between High-A Hudson Valley and Double-A Somerset.

Jackson, who turns 23 in eight days, slashed .262/.360/.459 with 41 stolen bases in 101 games across the two levels. He’s played an adequate shortstop, but has also gotten run at both second and third base. With Kilby on the roster, I can’t imagine he plays much shortstop this fall, even if both likely project as third basemen.

He was limited to just 101 games this year due to three very short stints on the injured list for minor ailments, which might be why he’s here. It could also be a big vote of confidence for an upper-minors infielder, who could be a good 2027 away from knocking on the door of the majors.

Our last Yankee heading to the desert is another 2025 draftee, and someone who managed to be one of the more unlikely 20/20 players you’ll ever see. Drafted in the 13th round out of West Virginia last year, it was a difficult debut season for West, who exclusively plays first base.

He slashed .226/.300/.394 with 20 home runs, 76 RBI, and 20 stolen bases in 124 games with Hudson Valley and suffered from a consistency issue. He’d have strong weeks, but immediately trade it with rough weeks. This is a guy who slugged .600 in the Big 12 just 18 months ago and was drafted for his slugging ability. The conditions in the AFL usually benefit offense, especially with the altitude. This guy could hit some moonshots if he gets a hold of one.

items.title: Saturday Posted & Toasted Notes: Wise men, French presidents, BrickBron James
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
Last weekend without basketball, fellas, so here’s a quick summary of a bunch of stuff that popped up recently around the NBA before we get down to (yeah, I know, , but still…) business.

  • James Wiseman has emerged as the early favorite for the Knicks’ 14th and likely final standard roster spot, according to the New York Post’s Stefan Bondy. Nothing new considering we’ve been talking about New York prioritizing a third center for months on end. In Bondy’s eyes, Tony Bradley and Drew Eubanks are Wiseman’s primary competition up front, while Bruce Brown and Ochai Agbaji are also fighting for the last spot in the Knicks’ roster.
  • Mike Brown, however, isn’t ready to declare Wiseman—or anybody else—the winner of that roster battle.

“I’m just going to let it unfold. I got no expectations. I’m not trying to forecast anything. I’m just taking this literally one practice at a time, one game at a time. And at the end of the day, when it comes time for us to figure out who’s going to be on the final roster, we’ll do it.”

  • The Athletic’s James L. Edwards III identified whether the Knicks can maintain their edge after winning the championship as New York’s biggest question entering the new season.
  • In another piece published over The Athletic, multiple reporters assembled three perspectives on the Knicks’ chances of repeating, and none were especially bullish.
  • Anne Hathaway would sacrifice another Oscar for another Knicks championship.
  • The Pistons and Jalen Duren finally found common ground, with the big boy and postseason no-shower inking a five-year, $200 million deal… without a weight clause on it.
  • Victor Wembanyama hasn’t even won an NBA title, but he’s already thinking about running for President of France.
  • It looks like the Las Vegas Whatevers are a very real thing and will get a franchise approved before Seattle does, but that could come with the con of having to wait an extra year to enter NBA play, contrary to the SuperSonics 2.0 making their comeback in time for the 2028-29 campaign.
  • JaVale McGee has joined the Shanghai Sharks, teaming up with D’Angelo Russell in China. Yes, that’s a real headline.
  • LeBron stans are already aboard the #lbjmvp train. Meanwhile…

items.title: 'We are a family, and it's really sad' – Nil Gimeno delivers a first win at Le Tour de Langkawi but it could well be Kern Pharma's last
items.author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
items.content:
A first win always means a lot, though somehow this one seems like it may mean that bit more, as when Nil Gimeno took his victory on stage 7 of Le Tour de Langkawi it was not just a beginning, but also potentially an end.

It was announced earlier this year that the Equipo Kern Pharma's main sponsor would be withdrawing at the end of the year, and while the search has long been on to find a new one, there has yet to be any good news announced. Sometimes the old adage that no news is good news doesn't ring true.

That means while the glee that the win had come for the 22-year-old Gimeno was written all over his face, so was the emotion when he contemplated what may be ahead for the squad where he built the foundation of his cycling career.

"I'm really, really happy to achieve this with this team," Gimeno told after going to podium in Batu Pahat to celebrate his win. "They've been really, really, really good with me, and also with all the riders. They care so much about us.

"These two years, they believed in me all the time. I had tough moments because pro cycling is really, really hard most of the time, and they were always there supporting me, saying to me that I have to believe in myself. And even though they are having a really, really bad moment now, I just want to say thank you to Juanjo [José Oroz, team manager] and Iosune [Murillo, coach], to all the staff members, to the riders.

"We are a family, and it's really sad that the team don't have any sponsor now, and we are doing everything we can to achieve that."

The support and camaraderie among the squad at the Tour de Langkawi was clearly visible in the scenes on the road in recent days, both when things were good, on Saturday, and not so good after Wednesday's stage 4. That was the day Gimeno had marked out as the one for him, and after third last year on the final stage he was determined to try and fight for more this time.

It started off well, he'd made the break and it looked like it was going to last but the rider, who knows how to deliver in a reduced group sprint, just fell short of making it to the line with the group of three to unfurl it.

"I did not have the best day, so I was really, really disappointed because it was a climb that treated me really good, and I did everything bad. I just was not there, so I was really, really sad," said Gimeno.

That was clear as he sat on the road after the line, with slumped shoulders and head, but his team rallied around, quietly offering moral support, an arm around the shoulder, a comforting word and watchful sympathetic eyes.

Equally, they were all there on Saturday, waiting patiently as Gimeno spoke to the broadcast media, so they could snatch a moment to celebrate together before he headed to the podium to stand on the top step, in a Kern Pharma jersey which looks set to disappear from the peloton.

The Spanish team has a long history, moving into the ProTeam ranks in 2020 but before that operating as a as a top feeder amateur team, Lizarte. Sports director Jon Armendariz, who was with the team at Le Tour de Langkawi ,has been there since well before the beginnings of its life as a ProTeam as his history with the squad that first came into existence in 1993 extends back 16 years. He started with Lizarte as a rider and then became a sports director.

"We don't know anything yet," Armendariz told before the winning move was made at the start of stage 7. "Juanjo, the team manager, is doing a very great job but the situation is complicated for us, and maybe these two stages will be our last stages in this team. We will see."

It's a sobering situation, with the Spanish team shepherding many riders into the pro ranks from both Spain and also beyond. Taiwan's Yen Yi Ho is a good example, with the rider who is now racing with the squad at Le Tour de Langkawi having spent this year in the ProTeam, learning the ropes of working within the team dynamics of a European-based squad after coming up the ranks at Equipo Finisher-Kern Pharma through the Giant Grassroots Program.

Then there is the Spanish rider Jorge Gutiérrez, a 24-year-old who has come up through the Equipo Kern Pharma development pathway before racing with the ProTeam the past three seasons. He had some health problems at the start of the season, but has come to Le Tour de Langkawi with some strong form, building on his tenth overall of last year and eight of 2024. Gutiérrez is now sitting at sixth on the GC with one stage to go and trying to make the most of the racing in Malaysia, despite the issues surrounding the team.

"It's a different situation. I've never lived this before," Gutiérrez told ahead of stage 7. "It's not easy, but I have to enjoy every competition day and appreciate how lucky we are as a team to be here."

Gutiérrez, who is the leading Kern Pharma rider on the overall, said before the penultimate stage that he was still looking for chances to move up higher, but also help his teammates chase opportunities. An hour after we spoke it was one of them, in the form of Gimeno, who capitalised on a big one.

The race is clearly also one that suits Gutiérrez, given his two finishes within the top ten overall, and even more so this year, with additional climbing thrown in. This time, however, the stakes at this race that plays to his strengths are higher than ever.

"I'm in a dangerous situation because I don't have a contract for next year, and I think I'm doing a good race, a good GC, and also I don't have problems helping my teammates for a victory, for staying in a breakaway," said Gutiérrez, "I hope for next year to have a contract and opportunity to be a cyclist. I love it."

That hope extends to the team, who earlier in the season gave riders and staff carte blanche to look for employment elsewhere given the situation. But for now, the wheels keep turning as there is a race and season to finish, and only after that will the thoughts of what's next be able to fully take over.

"We will come back to to Pamplona to our service course, and and we will see the situation and we'll see the best step for next year," concluded Gutiérrez.

*Cyclingnews attended Le Tour de Langkawi on an invitation/media package from the race that included travel and accommodation. In line with our editorial standards, our coverage is independent and was not subject to review, approval or influence by the organiser or any sponsor; no favourable coverage was promised or given in return.

items.title: Sparkassen Münsterland Giro: Olav Kooij comes out on top after chaotic crash marred bunch sprint
items.author: Lyne Lamoureux
items.content:
Olav Kooij (Decathlon CMA CGM) was the fastest in a hectic sprint to win the Sparkassen Münsterland Giro for the second time in his career, ahead of Jordi Meeus (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe). Frits Biesterbos (Picnic PostNL) was third in Münster.

The 24-year-old Dutch rider surged through chaotic final metres, with his leadout Cees Bol setting a fast pace, overtaking the other sprinters to have a clear shot to the line on German Unity Day.

No teams could control the front of the peloton once the early breakaway was reeled in on the second of three laps of the finishing circuits, with Visma-Lease A Bike, Lidl-Trek and Uno-X all taking turns to set the pace.

Lidl-Trek’s Mads Pedersen launched the sprint early, leading out his teammate Max Walscheid in his final race on German Unity Day. But they were quickly swarmed, and the German finished 12th.

“This is always a race with a really strong sprint field, and on the laps it's always quite hard to stay together. So also for us, it was not easy, but I think we managed to get in good position, and then actually the team helped me a lot. And then in the last 100 metres, Cees Bol came came to the front, and he kept the speed high. And I was in a position to launch myself. So when I went, I was just hoping to hold on,” Kooij said.

On the final lap, Kooij’s teammate Daan Hoole went from setting a hard pace at the front to getting a small gap, causing some excitement in the field.

“I was in his wheel, and I was like, ‘oh I needed to let a few guys in between,” Kooij said of the move. “But then I thought, like, ‘oh maybe I just had to gap and see how far he could go’. But it's really hard with the big roads in the last 3k. But I think was a nice try.”

“Just to win throughout the season, it's always really nice, and we hope to keep the momentum for the last races.”

For the first time, the race started in Borken, with the 196.6-kilometre route winding through the districts of Borken and Coesfeld before the traditional finish in front of Münster Castle. The key section came in the second half, with around 70 rolling kilometres through the Baumberge with several short, steep climbs. The terrain offered classics specialists a chance to put the sprinters under pressure. From there, roughly 50 mostly flat kilometres remained to Münster, where the race entered the familiar 4.3km city-centre circuit, which the men tackled three times.

Six riders escaped in the opening hour at the Sparkassen Münsterland Giro: Kelland O’Brien (Jayco Alula), Samuele Zoccarato (MBH Bank Ballan Telecom Fort), Ward Vanhoof (Flanders-Baloise), Samuel Leroux (TotalEnergies), Arno Wallenborn (Lotto-Kern Haus Outlet Montabaur) and Noe Ury (Foodmaker Gravelking), and they led for much of the day, including the small climbs in the rolling section.

Although there were a few attacks on those climbs, including the Gaststätte "Zum Coesfelder Berg and Daruper Berg, by Visma-Lease a Bike and Lidl-Trek, causing some brief chaos, the peloton stayed together. Alpecin-Premier Tech and Soudal Quick-Step kept the breakaway on a tight leash, allowing the gap to reach no more than two minutes.

The break, now down to five riders, had 10 seconds as they crossed the finish line to start the first of the three laps of the finishing circuits, and were finally caught inside six kilometres to go.

Teams jostled for control at the front on the flowy, twisty circuit, with Decathlon CMA CGM at the front to start the final lap, led by Dan Hoele, who took a brief solo flyer.

Teams such as Uno-X Mobility, Pinarello Q36.5, Visma-Lease a Bike all took turns at the front to try and control the pace but no real organisation could be seen.

items.title: Why Malaysia would be the perfect place for F1’s first wet-weather race in 2026
Yankees Birthday of the Day: Dave Winfield
items.author: Kento Mizuno
items.content:
Before Aaron Judge and Giancarlo Stanton, Dave Winfield (along with Dave Parker) was the definitive “Holy (bleep) that guy is huge!” star. Although his Yankees tenure was clouded by a tumultuous relationship with George Steinbrenner, Winfield deserves to be remembered as a great Yankee who made those 80s teams memorable despite never winning a ring.

: October 3, 1951 (St. Paul, MN): 1981-90

Winfield’s athletic abilities were already quite apparent in his youth. He starred in both baseball and basketball in high school and college. Following his time at the University of Minnesota, he was drafted by teams from not one, not two, but three pro leagues — in addition to MLB’s Padres and the NBA’s Atlanta Hawks, the NFL’s Minnesota Vikings took a flier on Winfield even though he hadn’t played college football. Thankfully, the hulking phenom chose the diamond.

The Padres thrust Winfield into the fire, having him skip the minor leagues entirely and placing him on their major league roster. While he wasn’t exactly a star from the word go, he was a productive regular almost immediately, hitting .277/.331/.383 (106 wRC+) across 154 PAs in 1973 as a 21 year-old. 

From there, Winfield continued to steadily improve, going from 1.9 WAR in ‘74, to 2.8 in ‘75, and 4.6 in ‘76. In 1977, he earned his first All-Star selection; he returned to the Midsummer Classic every year from then on until 1988. His pièces de résistance came in 1979, when he slashed .308/.395/.558 (161 wRC+) with 34 homers and a league-leading 118 RBI while winning a Gold Glove in right field. His 7.8 WAR paced the National League, even though he finished 3rd in MVP voting. Bet all the keyboard warriors were furi- oh right they didn’t exist back then. 

All this was more than enough to catch the eye of George Steinbrenner, who was eager to add another ring after consecutive titles in ‘77 and ‘78. In December 1980, the Yankees made Winfield the richest player in baseball with a ten-year, $23 million contract. Winfield almost made the Boss’ dream come true in ‘81, posting a 139 wRC+ in the strike-shortened regular season before showing out on both sides of the ball in the ALDS and ALCS. Here’s the large baseball man robbing Tony Armas of a home run in ALCS Game 2:

However, the season ended on a sour note for Winfield and the Yankees. The Dodgers won the World Series in six games, and Winfield was limited to just one hit in 22 at bats. In a show of poor comedic timing, he asked for the ball after his lone hit, a single. Needless to say, this did not sit well with George Steinbrenner, and the two would become bitter enemies for the remainder of Winfield’s time in the Bronx.

The 1981 season would be the Yankees’ only postseason appearance during Winfield’s tenure. However, that was no fault of Winfield’s, who kept producing at a high level well into his thirties. Although modern defensive metrics suggest that his sterling defensive reputation at the time wasn’t wholly deserved, there is absolutely no doubt about the quality of his bat.

In terms of batting average, Winfield’s best year came in 1984, when he locked horns with a young Don Mattingly for the AL batting title. The teammates were tied going into the very last game of the season, but Mattingly won the title by going 4-for-5, raising his average to .343, while Winfield went 1-for-4, finishing the year at a .340 clip. Here’s a clip of him from that year showing not only his sheer strength, but the impressive plate coverage that allowed him to hit for such a high average:

On the other hand, saber-enthusiasts like me would point to 1988 as Winfield’s best season in pinstripes. That year, he slashed .322/.398/.530 for a 157 wRC+, the fourth-highest mark in the majors. What makes this even more impressive is that he did this at 36 years old. To put this into context, Giancarlo Stanton was in his age-35 season when he surprised us all by posting a 157 wRC+ in 77 games last year. Now imagine him being just as good this year, except over a full season. Can you? I certainly can’t. Among all qualified seasons by batters aged 36 or above since 1947, Winfield’s 1988 ranks 19th, tied with 1971 Willie Mays and 2001 Edgar Martinez.

All told, in his time as a Yankee, Winfield hit .290/.356/.495 with 205 homers and 818 RBI. No matter how you slice it, he was worth every penny of his contract. And yet, George Steinbrenner, famously afflicted with a severe case of “what have you done for me lately”-brain, made it his personal mission to antagonize Winfield at every turn.

In 1985, after the Yankees faded late in the season and ceded the division lead to the Toronto Blue Jays, the cantankerous owner derided Winfield in the papers, saying, “Where is Reggie Jackson? We need a Mr. October or a Mr. September. Winfield is Mr. May.” In 1987, Steinbrenner began to withhold payments owed to Winfield to be donated to the Winfield Foundation, founded in 1977 to provide relief and opportunities to struggling families in his hometown of St. Paul. Steinbrenner accused Winfield of misappropriating funds for personal gain, circulating unfounded reports in the media in an attempt to undermine the star player’s credibility.

Ultimately, Steinbrenner would ruin himself in his quest to tarnish Winfield’s name. The Yankees owner made a deal with gambler and alleged Mafia associate Howie Spira, paying him $40,000 in exchange to dig up dirt on Winfield. Spira publicly accused Winfield of betting on baseball, and commissioner Fay Vincent launched an investigation. However, no evidence was found of Winfield ever betting on baseball; what uncovered was Steinbrenner’s clandestine deal with Spira. Vincent ordered Steinbrenner to resign as general partner of the Yankees and banned him from team operations for three years, and that was that.

At that point, Winfield had had more than enough. In May 1990, he waived his no-trade clause and accepted a trade to the California Angels, where he would play the following season as well. In 1992, at 40 years of age, Winfield played a crucial role on the championship-winning Blue Jays, hitting 26 homers and driving in 108 in the regular season, and coming up with the decisive blow in Game 6 of the World Series, an 11th-inning, two-run double. So much for the “Mr. May” moniker!

After three more years in the majors, two with his hometown Twins and one final year with Cleveland, Winfield called it quits. His career numbers are truly staggering; 465 homers, 3110 hits, and a .283/.353/.475 line over 23 seasons. In 2001, in his first year of eligibility, he was elected to the Hall of Fame.

Dave Winfield was a truly elite player who shone brightly in the Bronx. It’s a shame that he only had one chance to play in the postseason as a Yankee, but that shouldn’t cloud our appraisal of what he contributed to this franchise. For the better part of a decade, Winfield provided Yankee fans with top-level play, even as his teams could not quite reach October. He deserves to be remembered as one of the Yankees’ best free agent signings of all time, and just simply as a Yankees great.

See more of the “Yankees Birthday of the Day” series here.

items.title: UEC European Championships: 'I just really love winning' - Demi Vollering claims solo elite women's victory for dominant Dutch team
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
Demi Vollering took her first win in the rainbow jersey on Saturday, the Dutch rider defending her women's road race title at the European Championships in Slovenia, proving her status as the dominant rider in the women’s sport.

Attacking on the final climb, with 14.km to go, the Dutch rider quickly took a 20-second lead on two riders, which included one of her Dutch teammates, inevitably growing that advantage in the closing kilometres.

Initially Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney (Poland) was left to chase on her own, Puck Pieterse rightly sitting on, but even when they were joined by Elisa Longo-Borghini (Italy), Antonia Niedermaier (Germany) and world time trial champion Marlen Reusser (Switzerland), a coordinated pursuit took time to materialise.

While the chase did begin to cut the deficit, Vollering had done enough to take a second title of her career and extend the Dutch dominance in the event, which had only one winner from outside the country in the championship’s 11 editions.

With Pieterse able to sit on in the chasing group, she was able to win the sprint for second place, making for a Dutch one-two, crossing the line five seconds behind her compatriot, while Reusser took the final podium place. Niewiadoma-Phinney’s bid for a medal was brought to an unfortunate end with a crash on the final corner.

Vollering’s win came not just off the back of her own efforts, but with the benefit of brilliant teamwork for the Dutch. With a two-woman break up the road, they did the lion’s share of the chasing, before executing the perfect tactical plan on the closing circuit, which included the brutal climb to Možjanca.

"It's crazy, and also a beautiful second place for Puck today. So I think we can be very proud of her effort again," Vollering said when asked about the Dutch dominance in the event.

"I just really love winning, and it never gets boring for me. So I think also it's not only the winning for me, but just improving yourself and getting better every day, working on yourself every day, and see what's still possible for the future. I think that's what I love most about this about this job."

Vollering will close her season at the European time trial on Wednesday.

In only its 11th edition, the Elite women’s road race at the 2026 European Championships took on a 130km route, starting in the Slovenian capital, Ljubljana and finishing in Šenčur. With a long, looping opening leg north, the race then tackled two laps of a 22km clockwise circuit around the finish town, and though each included the tough climb to Možjanca, the top came 14km from the line, allowing opportunities for a regrouping on the plateau, descent and flat run in.

After a long neutralised opening, the attacks came the moment the flag dropped, though the Dutch team quickly brought them to heel. However, Carina Schrempf (Austria) and Margot Vanpachtenbeke (Belgium) soon got away and were allowed their leads, though they were soon chased by home rider Nika Bobnar. She was unable to make an impact, though the French team were particularly keen to get up the road, but their aggression was stymied when one of their number crashed on a right-hand bend.

This calmed the action in the bunch and the leading duo were allowed to extend their advantage, taking almost two minutes into the closing 100km, the Dutch team, containing newly crowned World Champion Demi Vollering, taking control. With Lorena Wiebes working on the front of the pack, the gap was gently whittled away, dropping to less than 1:20 with 70km to go.

It was here that Kristýna Burlová (Czechia) made a move to bridge the gap, the peloton dropping back and the gap increasing. However, as the circuit approached, the peloton naturally sped up, especially with the Italians, Swiss and Polish all upping the pace, and not only was Burlová caught, but the break was also tagged before the first ascent of the climb to Možjanca began.

Femke de Vries set a blistering pace for much of the climb, and by the time she was dropped close to the top, only seven riders remained at the front with 36km to go. On the plateau, Marlen Reusser (Switzerland) put in a speculative attack, but when that was closed by Vollering, the leading group settled until the descent, where Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney attacked.

Reusser had another go when the Polish rider was brought back, but it was the chasing group who had the biggest impact, Cecilie Uttrup Ludwig (Denmark) and Franziska Koch (Germany) going straight past and building an advantage. However, the favourites’ group had, by then, swollen to 17 riders, including five Dutch women in that bunch.

Uttrup Ludwig and Koch led by 20 seconds as they crossed the finish line with one 22km lap to go, but the Dutch squad had other ideas and began to drag them back again. With the two leaders back in the pack shortly afterwards, the Germans played another card, this time Liane Lippert attacking, but with Noemi Rüegg and De Vries on her wheel working for Reusser and Vollering respectively, she received little help.

They were caught at the bottom of the climb, and it was a case of deja vu, De Vries setting the pace for Vollering, in a group of five, from which Reusser had been dropped. With Puck Pieterse taking De Vries’s place and lifting the speed even more, only Vollering and Niewiadoma-Phinney remained. But both were dropped when Vollering made her move with 14.5km left to race.

items.title: Giro dell'Emilia: Davide Piganzoli takes victory after perfectly timed attack in final five kilometres
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
Davide Piganzoli won a pulsating edition of the Giro dell’Emilia on Saturday, the Visma-Lease a Bike rider attacking on the descent before the final climb of San Luca to win alone.

Behind him, Tom Pidcock (Q36.5) put in a dogged fight to take second place, three seconds behind, with Oscar Onley (Netcompany-Ineos) in third.

Piganzoli had been towed onto the back of a three-man group by Pidcock on the descent of the penultimate of five ascents of the San Luca climb, then escaped late on the descent. With his teammate Matteo Jorgenson in the chasing group, the pursuit took time to form and was far from concerted, with the Italian leading by 15 seconds at the bottom of the final climb.

Much of the chase was left to Pidcock, but the British rider struggled to close the gap, only coming close when Onley made a move, but by then the victory was PIganzoli’s, the 24-year-old taking a sixth career win.

In its 109th edition, the Giro dell’Emilia took on a 197.9k route starting in Ferrara and closing with its traditional finish up the legendary San Luca climb in Bologna. Indeed, that ascent, and its screaming tifosi, would feature five times, the race taking on four frantic nine-kilometre laps to close the day.

The route was mostly flat for the opening 100km, only then did the road begin to rise to Loiano, the climb covering 6.6km with an average gradient of 5.7%. After that, the Salita di Via Belvedere presented a 1.8km test at over 9.2%, before the road headed north to the finish on the outskirts of Bologna.

After an active start, eight riders escaped up the road. Amanuel Ghebreigzabhier (Lidl-Trek), Ådne Holter (UNO-X Mobility), Manuele Tarozzi (Bardiani-CSF 7Saber), Diego Pablo Sevilla (Polti-Visit Malta), Ben Granger, Tommaso Nencini (both Solution Tech Nippo Rali) and the General Store-Essegibi-F.Lli Curia pair of Andrii Ponomar and Kevin Mezzo Rosola soon built a lead.

That advantage stuck resolutely around the two-minute mark, with the peloton not allowing them too much more, and as they passed the halfway mark they sat only 2:20 ahead. However, over the top of the Loiano climb, the lead began to drop.

With the lead just over one minute, the Salita di Via Belvedere proved the undoing of the breakaway, the group beginning to split as the peloton closed in. Though their advantage steadied for a while, with the first ascent of San Luca fast approaching, the peloton were flying, the leaders less than 20 seconds ahead at the bottom and caught well before the top.

A brief truce followed, but before the top the action kicked off again, and a group of six took a small lead through the finish line, though they were never allowed to build any kind of meaningful advantage. Only three remained when they crossed the line after the second ascent of San Luca, though the chasing peloton was significantly smaller than the one they’d attacked, but the race was back together shortly afterwards.

The next ascent saw the race truly explode, Matteo Jorgenson (Visma-Lease a Bike) launching a move which World Champion Brandon McNulty (UAE Team Emirates) countered. On the descent, the race reformed slightly, though McNulty’s team had three men in a 16-man group and began playing their cards, with Jhonatan Narváez attacking repeatedly.

However, the race was in a constant state of flux with repeated attacks onto the penultimate climb, where Jorgenson attacked yet again, further thinning the group and crossing the line with Ben Healy (EF Education-EasyPost) and Oscar Onley (Netcompany-Ineos) as Tom Pidcock (Pinarello-Q36.5) chased desperately.

With Davide Piganzoli glued to his wheel, Pidcock caught the leading trio on the descent, but Piganzoli soon made his race-winning move.

items.title: How the FIA plans to differentiate between Rally1 and Rally2 in WRC 2027
The former weakness key to Red Bull's sudden supremacy
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
While Mercedes’ troubled upgrade removed it as a factor, Red Bull’s rivals see signs in its maiden pole position as an engine manufacturer of a proper shuffle in Formula 1's competitive order.

Max Verstappen’s first pole since last year’s title-deciding Abu Dhabi Grand Prix certainly owed nothing to good fortune. He was quickest in all three qualifying segments. Proof of the RB22’s pace was made firm with Isack Hadjar ending up third on the timesheets.

But it is not the Red Bull result that has surprised the opposition. Instead, it is how it was achieved.

A deep dive into the telemetry data of where the pace has come from suggests a reset in the performance profile of the top squads – with areas where teams had previously been strong no longer true this weekend.

As detailed below, on the Sepang straights Verstappen was super strong, while in the high-speed and medium-speed corners where Red Bull was being murdered by the other frontrunners earlier in the year, it was now right up there.

This points to Red Bull having addressed the key weaknesses that had held it back.

It has got more out of its all-new 2026 power units and, rivals suspect, its Baku upgrade unleashed far more potential from the car in areas where it was lagging that had been on show in Azerbaijan.

There is no single magic bullet in F1 that ever leapfrogs a team forward, and observing Red Bull’s form over the season points to it having just steadily chipped away.

Miami and Austria upgrades addressed some of its high- and medium-speed corner deficit. So, with more getting unleashed from better energy management too, by Madrid – a track with a good mixture of high, medium and low speed corners, it was within touching distance of pole as Verstappen missed out there by 0.140 seconds.

Its Baku upgrade had not shown itself to be a game-changing last weekend, especially with Verstappen having been slowed by power unit problems.

But the layout of the circuit there is all about low speed and straights – and the pace on Sunday showed how close it was.

So it was only in Malaysia, where there is a much better combination of high- and medium-speed corners, that the true potential of that upgrade has perhaps emerged.

McLaren boss Andrea Stella certainly thinks that there has been a change of trend here, which he hints may have come from a "significant step" Red Bull’s Baku upgrade gave it.

Asked by The Race about whether he had seen a change in the performance profile of the top squads, he said: “It's interesting here in Malaysia to see that the straightline speed advantage that Mercedes had in Baku, we don't see it. It's kind of disappeared.

“The best performance in a straightline seems to be, by a decent margin, Red Bull. The best cornering performance is Ferrari. And we, McLaren…are also puzzled a little bit by the fact that in high speed, we are no longer the best car, like we seemed to be in Madrid, or we seemed to be in Zandvoort.”

Verstappen himself concurred that Red Bull’s recent upgrades had “pushed some of the weaknesses out of the car” as he suggested this result was simply down to the team having understood its car a lot better.

With increased downforce comes more grip and a better balance – and a virtuous circle with the gains that then come from the tyres.

Plus, added Verstappen: “on a track probably where it’s all very hot and you want a stable balance or connected balance, then that’s very important. And that’s, I think, what we have found a little bit more over the last weekends".

It was interesting to hear Hadjar talk about how, when he returned to the car in Baku, it felt different to when he had last raced before the summer break.

“I definitely feel like I jumped in a car that’s way better than when I left it in Budapest,” he said. “Definitely, when you step out actually for three races and you come back, you actually notice a bigger difference.”

Yet despite what everyone has seen of Red Bull this weekend, there remain a few caveats before suggesting this is the start of a new chapter in the F1 2026 season.

Mercedes falling back may be a one-off, plus Malaysia’s heat and rough surface make it an outlier – both in terms of tyre management and set-up and aero characteristics that include cooling compromises.

So the proof of where things stand up may have to wait until Singapore next weekend.

How Verstappen beat Hamilton to pole

What really stood out about Verstappen’s pole position lap was the level of confidence visible from the onboard footage. I can’t remember an occasion in 2026 when he’s looked so at one with the car, so it was no surprise that he referred to its “connected balance”.

He could brake late, turn in decisively, and on the few occasions when the car required any corrective action, he was able to do it quickly and with the minimum of fuss. 

That said, it wasn’t in the corners that Verstappen built his decisive advantage. There, it was about getting the most out of a package that is significantly improved but still usually not market-leading in turns. Where he could make hay was on the straights and in the braking zones.

Although Verstappen’s pole position margin was three-tenths of a second over Hamilton, the battle for pole position only swung decisively in his favour in the final sector. There, he was a mighty 0.464s quicker than closest rival Lewis Hamilton.

The strong straightline speed of the RB22 showed immediately at the start of the lap, gaining around a tenth over Hamilton (with a similar margin over the McLaren of Lando Norris and Kimi Antonelli’s Mercedes) by the first corner based on when all were at 100% throttle. Relative to Hamilton, he emerged from Turn 2 with a similar advantage and by the end of the first sector, 145 metres before Turn 4, he had a 0.138s edge over Hamilton - and just over three-tenths over both Antonelli and Norris.

Sector 2 was the weak point for the Red Bull, the fast, flowing section bookended by slow corners where the battle swung towards Hamilton - who generally registered a similar or higher minimum speed in this section and took 0.304s out of Verstappen - putting him 0.166s up entering the final sector. 

Much of the final sector is at full throttle, and it was here that Verstappen demolished Hamilton by 0.464s on his pole lap - although it should be noted that Leclerc was actually the faster Ferrari driver through here with a deficit to the Red Bull of only 0.2s. 

Although Hamilton was a little quicker in the Turn 11 right-hander than Verstappen, this sector was mainly Red Bull territory.

This all added up to an emphatic pole position after a performance that was all about Verstappen being at his brilliant best in the corners in an improved car that gave him the balance he needed and cashing in on the straights.

items.title: "The FIA needs to step in" - Russell's cooling vest comments explained
Yankees must slay the three-headed monster atop the Rays lineup
items.author: Peter Brody
items.content:
This is where things get down to the brass tacks. The Yankees swept the Red Sox aside in the AL Wild Card Series, boat racing Boston by a combined score of 18-2, to fly into the ALDS with belief and positive momentum. It’s a whole other beast they’ll face in the Rays, their offense rolling into the postseason in far better shape than the Red Sox.

The Rays raced out to an AL-best 98 wins, significantly outperforming their Pythagorean win-loss thanks to one of the most well-rounded approaches in baseball. Despite sitting middle of the pack in runs per game (4.54) and slugging (.402), Tampa Bay’s offense still finished with the fifth-best wRC+ (104). Their offense has a clear identity built around power at the top, speed, and bat-to-ball prowess. They struck out the least (18.8-percent) of any team in MLB, which helps explain how they tied with the Brewers for the league lead in batting average (.258), and when paired with their AL-leading 164 stolen bases allows them to get the most out of the traffic they generate.

The ever consistent Yandy Díaz leads things off, coming off his fifth-straight season with at least a 120 wRC+. He played 154 games, slashing .293/.359/.446 with 22 home runs, 85 RBI, 93 runs scored, and a 125 wRC+ while continuing to be almost impossible to whiff and strike out. He has hurt the Yankees his whole career and that was especially true in 2026, when he batted .362 with a .944 OPS and 154 wRC+ in 51 plate appearances. The lone holes in his swing are against high-spin four-seamers from right handers up and in or middle-away, a pitch which Games 1 & 2 starters Gerrit Cole and Cam Schlittler specialize in.

Jonathan Aranda bats second coming off a season in which he batted .274/.358/.434 with 22 home runs, 92 RBI, 73 runs scored, and a 123 wRC+. However, the Yankees had his number all season, holding him to a paltry .427 OPS and 15 wRC+ in 47 plate appearances as they were able to strike him out 34-percent of the time. He has shown a willingness to chase the fastball above the zone, which happens to be a weapon pitch for all four of the starters the Yankees plan to roll out.

Those two set the table for the scariest threat in the Rays lineup: Junior Caminero. The third baseman became just the second player in MLB history after Eddie Matthews to post consecutive 40 home run seasons before turning 23. He added patience to his game in 2026, almost doubling his career walk rate to finish with a .276/.360/.524 triple slash line, 42 homers, 101 RBI, 100 runs scored, a 142 wRC+ and 5.3 fWAR while posting the highest average bat speed in the league. He holds his own against almost every pitch but does most of his damage against the heater and breaking ball. Just three of his home runs have come against the off-speed so I expect the likes of Max Fried and Carlos Rodón to feed him a steady diet of changeups down and away. Encouragingly, the Yankees were one of the few teams that managed to rein him in — in 54 plate appearances he managed just a .565 OPS and 51 wRC+ with Yankees pitchers getting him to pop it up on over 30-percent of his batted balls.

MLB stolen base leader Chandler Simpson figures to bat in the middle of the order. He was the only qualified hitter in 2026 to not hit a homer, but was also one of just seven qualified hitters to bat above .300, his 7.8-percent strikeout rate second-lowest in baseball. He’s joined in the middle of the order by Victor Mesa Jr., the rookie acquired from the Marlins over the winter and promoted mid-season to hit 14 home runs with a 128 wRC+ and 2.6 fWAR in just 79 games. Generally batting ninth is shortstop Taylor Walls, whose 74 wRC+ at first glance wouldn’t scare you yet he has managed to be a thorn in the Yankees’ side with a 120 wRC+ in 111 plate appearances over the last four years.

For the rest of the spots in the lineup, the Rays tend to go with a strict platoon. Liam Hicks usually bats cleanup against righties, the catcher posting a 130 wRC+ with as many walks as strikeouts since joining the Rays from the Marlins at the deadline, while Nick Fortes tends to start against southpaws. At second base, Richie Palacios owns a 113 wRC+ against righties while Ryan Vilade owns a 126 wRC+ against lefties. In center, Cedric Mullins is probably the one guaranteed soft landing spot against righties with his 80 wRC+, while Jonny DeLuca is a far more potent weapon when a lefty is on the mound (114 wRC+).

Put together, Kevin Cash can rely on guaranteed production at the top of the lineup while a deep bench gives him the opportunity to mix and match depending on the matchup. He has shown all season that he remains one of the best managers at putting his players in the best positions to succeed thus squeezing every drop out of the true talent level of the roster. You know the Rays are going to do all the little things right — taking the extra base, moving the runner over, getting the run in from home with less than two outs — which makes the three-headed monster atop the lineup their X-factor in this series.

items.title: McLaren puzzled by persistent Norris-only F1 car problem
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
Lando Norris has a straightline speed deficit to team-mate Oscar Piastri for the second Formula 1 weekend running in Malaysia, one his McLaren team doesn’t understand. 

Norris struggled with a small straightline deficit on his McLaren in Baku versus Piastri, because of an issue that the team suspected was linked to fuel injection in the power unit. 

That deficit is still present at Sepang where Norris was over six tenths off pole in qualifying sixth, albeit 0.005s ahead of Piastri. 

"I felt like my lap was very strong…I'm still struggling a lot in the straights everywhere. I'm just down on every single straight," Norris said. 

"Every time I get a good exit, I'm just slower in the end of the straight. It just hurts seeing this every single time, so I should be higher up, not because I could have done a better job necessarily, but just because we're not getting everything out of the car that we need to. 

"That doesn't [just] make my life tough today, but it also makes it tough for tomorrow."

The straightline speed deficit between Norris (white line) and Piastri (orange line) in qualifying is clear when you look at the data for the second half of their fastest Q3 laps. 

"We should say that the issue we see on Lando’s car is about a lack of straightline speed," McLaren team boss Andrea Stella confirmed after qualifying. 

"So we see that in the power limited section, the car accelerates a little less and develops a little bit less top speed, all the other parameters being the same. We talk about probably between one and two kph, like they are small quantities. 

"They are even difficult to see because as soon as Lando, for instance, has a little bit of slipstream from a car four seconds ahead, now you see Lando faster than the other car. 

"It’s small quantities that we see statistically and we should more precisely talk about the deficit of straightline speed. OK, which we can quantify in a laptime loss that I would say in excess of one tenth of a second, possibly between one and two tenths of a second."

McLaren doesn’t understand what’s behind the issue and it won’t be able to fix it until the next race in Singapore at the earliest, meaning Norris will have to suffer with it through this grand prix. 

"[It’s a] different conversation is about why that is and why we can talk immediately about a lack of power," Stella added.

"In reality, there can be different reasons. It's more difficult to monitor what is happening from a power unit point of view because if it was deployment, we would be able to see it possibly has to do with some other parameters.

"But at the same time, there's behaviours of the power unit that depend on what's happening on the chassis side. 

"Finally, there could be parameters that have to do with the drag of the car.

"So it's at no point we are making a point about power unit. We are just making a point about a lack of straightline speed, which we want to make a point about because it's fair to Lando that we take the responsibility for the fact that on his car, there's a laptime deficit, which at the moment we have not been able to remove in a couple of events.

"But obviously, we are definitely looking at all the possible parameters, and we will look at further changes, but we only can do that now for Singapore."

AL Division Series Game 1 Preview: New York Yankees @ Tampa Bay Rays
items.author: Estevão Maximo
items.content:
Sweeping the Red Sox with two blowout wins was a joyous occasion, not to mention the tangible positive impact of setting up your rotation for the ALDS. The Yankees can begin the series against the Rays with Gerrit Cole as the Game 1 starter, which is only fitting considering Cole’s regular-season campaign in 2026 began and ended against the Rays, both times with a quality start.

Making his postseason debut this season, Cole will get the ball after nearly a week and a half off, his longest time between starts since returning from injury. In three appearances against the AL East champs in the regular season—the most he had against any single team—Cole averaged six innings and delivered a 2.50 ERA, enjoying success against a team not known for its home run pedigree.

Having last played a competitive meaningful game well before the end of the regular season, the Rays will set out to prove there is no rust in their game with Drew Rasmussen starting Game 1. Who better to represent what the Rays are all about than Rasmussen, acquired for the power-hitting Willy Adames as a swingman/backend starter, only to turn into one of the more dominant starters in the AL?

The postseason scenario and all that it entails could be seen as an opportunity to test the Rays’ resolve when it comes to their ace. Rasmussen was already dominant last season—part of what held him back from entering the conversation with the big boys was just how carefully managed he was by the Rays, who only let him reach or surpass 90 pitches twice in 2025. This year, Rasmussen has done that 17 times, including a career-high 114 pitches in a win over the Yankees just a couple of weeks ago—one in which perhaps the Rays gave a sign of their intentions with a trial run. With this extra leeway, Rasmussen managed to pitch 22 more innings than last season despite having one fewer start (31 to 30).

Rasmussen’s ability to go deeper into games than what we’re accustomed to seeing not only from him but also from the Rays as a team is of great value—especially if we are to read into regular season numbers. As much as the Yankees may have a better rotation, perhaps the biggest advantage in this series is in the bullpen. While New York had the second-lowest bullpen ERA in baseball, Tampa was only number 14. The key here, particularly looking at the postseason and a matchup with the Yankees lineup, is that the 95 home runs allowed by the Rays’ bullpen represented the third-highest mark in the bigs.

Then again, this is a Tampa team with the benefit of off-days between each of the first three games. One can only imagine how aggressive they might be willing to go with the likes of Bryan Baker, Cam Booser, and Kevin Kelly. While Baker is the closer, Booser gets the nod as the X-factor for the Rays in Game 1 and this series as a whole—the Yankees were 1-for-10 against him in the regular season, the one being an Austin Wells home run.

Booser’s importance stems from a complete lack of southpaw options for a team whose only other left-hander who finished the season on the active roster was Steven Matz. Garrett Cleavinger was cleared to be a part of the ALDS roster, but his 2026 numbers were quite bad, with an 89 ERA+ in 41.1 innings.

Unlike the Red Sox, all the Rays’ top starters are right-handers, allowing Aaron Boone to utilize his lefty-heavy lineup without fear, starting in Game 1 against Rasmussen. And if Booser can’t shut them down out of the bullpen, Tampa all of a sudden has an incredibly difficult mission to contain Ben Rice, Cody Bellinger, Luis García Jr., and company.
